definition: Authorize means to give official permission for something to be done — a go-ahead granted before the act, by someone whose position carries that power.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word authorize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know authorize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The city council authorized the night market for one trial summer, over the parking committee's objections.
Allowing something is weaker than authorizing it: anyone can allow by simply not objecting, while to authorize takes an office — a signature or a vote that actively grants the permission.
A mandate goes further than authorizing: a board that authorizes repairs lets the crews proceed, but a board that mandates them makes the work compulsory — permission hardened into command.

To empower is to hand someone a lasting capacity to act — a law can empower an agency for a generation. Authorize is narrower and more transactional: it grants official permission for a particular act, and it can be as small as one signature clearing one purchase.

To sanction is to give official approval with a blessing flavor, often to something already arranged — a league sanctions a tournament. Authorize stands at the front door: it is the advance permission that lets the act happen at all. (Watch the trap: sanction can also mean to penalize; authorize never flips.)

Authorize means to give official permission for something to be done — a go-ahead granted before the act, by someone whose position carries that power.

For two years the observatory's staff asked to open the roof deck for public star nights, and the request died on desk after desk — until the new director finally authorized it, adding a single condition beside her signature: railings first.
Authorize is official through and through: not agreement, not encouragement, but formal permission granted by someone whose position holds that power.

The director's signature is what turns star nights from a wish into a sanctioned program — the same Latin auctor, 'originator,' that gives us author: to authorize an act is to stand behind it as its official source.
Authorize is the paperwork verb of offices and agencies: budgets, permits, launches, missions.
Two things travel with it.
First, standing — only someone whose position holds the power can authorize, which is why a friend agrees to your plan while a board authorizes it.
Second, timing — authorization comes first, clearing the road ahead; approval of a text already drafted and signed wants a different verb (treaties are ratified).
People are authorized to act — 'authorized personnel only' — and the noun authorization names the grant itself.

For thirty years, anyone wanting to drill a well in Harlan County has started at a single metal desk in the courthouse basement.
That desk belongs to Ruth Okafor, the county clerk whose office must authorize every new well before a drill bit touches the ground.
The power is not hers personally; it comes with the seal.
State law names her office, not her, as the one that can grant permission.
Farmers sometimes grumble that a neighbor's nod ought to be enough.
Ruth points to the aquifer maps and shakes her head.
Permission here is not politeness, she says.
It is an official act, given in advance, and recorded — or the well does not exist.
